prior_art.basis: Independent review by claude-independent-prior-art-reviewer-20261106: No AI system has made a Nobel-worthy discovery without human guidance, so the Main KPI of 1 autonomous Nobel-worthy discovery is unmet. The strongest open systems reach workshop level: Sakana's open-source AI Scientist-v2 submitted three fully autonomous manuscripts to an ICLR workshop and one exceeded the average human acceptance threshold (https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2504.08066). Kosmos runs up to 12 hours on a human-supplied objective and dataset; independent scientists judged 79.4% of its statements accurate, and of seven highlighted findings three reproduced unpublished results and four were new (https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2511.02824). Google's Co-Scientist (Nature 2026, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10644-y) works with human scientists. A 2026 critique argues agentic AI scientists are not built for autonomous discovery (https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.08956). Open code is plentiful (SakanaAI/AI-Scientist about 14,950 stars, AI-Scientist-v2 about 7,446). Class neutral: large potential benefit, but autonomous discovery systems raise dual-use and verification risks. Honest limit: running the open AI Scientist or Kosmos-style loops is a known baseline and not new work, and Nobel-worthiness cannot be attested quickly by checkers; tasks must be bounded, checkable steps such as an autonomous result independently replicated and judged new by domain experts.
